LLMs systematically fail to uphold commutativity, with violations in up to 20% of problem pairs.
LLMs break down under notation invariance, with accuracy collapsing (e.g., from 99.81% to 7.51%) when digits are replaced by novel symbols.
Providing explicit rules via prompting often degrades performance, while explain-and-do prompts merely maintain baseline accuracy.
Fine-tuning (SFT) improves numeric accuracy but fails to generalize to symbolic tasks, while RL-based methods show better generalization but lower numeric performance.
future_direction: Develop new diagnostic benchmarks for rule learning
Innovate model architectures and training methods for genuine mathematical reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve impressive results on advanced mathematics benchmarks but sometimes fail on basic arithmetic tasks, raising the question of whether they have truly grasped fundamental arithmetic rules or are merely relying on pattern matching. To unravel this issue, we systematically probe LLMs' understanding of two-integer addition ($0$ to $2^{64}$) by testing three crucial properties: commutativity ($A+B=B+A$), representation invariance via symbolic remapping (e.g., $7 \mapsto Y$), and consistent accuracy scaling with operand length. Our evaluation of 12 leading LLMs reveals a stark disconnect: while models achieve high numeric accuracy (73.8-99.8%), they systematically fail these diagnostics. Specifically, accuracy plummets to $\le 7.5$% with symbolic inputs, commutativity is violated in up to 20% of cases, and accuracy scaling is non-monotonic. Interventions further expose this pattern-matching reliance: explicitly providing rules degrades performance by 29.49%, while prompting for explanations before answering merely maintains baseline accuracy. These findings demonstrate that current LLMs address elementary addition via pattern matching, not robust rule induction, motivating new diagnostic benchmarks and innovations in model architecture and training to cultivate genuine mathematical reasoning. Our dataset and generating code are available at https://github.com/kuri-leo/llm-arithmetic-diagnostic.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How does arithmetic ability work in large language models, and why do only a few attention heads significantly impact arithmetic performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, constructs an internal logic chain with four stages, and applies CNA to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic operations, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons' coefficient scores, and applies the method for model pruning and bias editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability resides in a limited number of attention heads, with each head specializing in distinct operations.
CNA identifies an internal logic chain from input to prediction with four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
The method can be used for model pruning on arithmetic tasks, achieving good performance with only 5% of deep FFN neurons.
The method can identify and edit FFN neurons to reduce gender bias in model outputs.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which lacks complete theoretical foundation.
Lack of standardization across attribution methods; gradient-based and SHAP methods are computationally expensive.
Potential risk that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to maliciously change model outputs.
future_direction: Further investigation of why multiplication heads do not significantly impact accuracy.
Exploration of the method on different gender bias datasets.
Investigating how to distinguish whether a model has been edited maliciously.
papers.abstract: We find arithmetic ability resides within a limited number of attention heads, with each head specializing in distinct operations. To delve into the reason, we introduce the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method, which identifies an internal logic chain consisting of four distinct stages from input to prediction: feature enhancing with shallow FFN neurons, feature transferring by shallow attention layers, feature predicting by arithmetic heads, and prediction enhancing among deep FFN neurons. Moreover, we identify the human-interpretable FFN neurons within both feature-enhancing and feature-predicting stages. These findings lead us to investigate the mechanism of LoRA, revealing that it enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of FFN neurons related to predictions. Finally, we apply our method in model pruning for arithmetic tasks and model editing for reducing gender bias. Code is on https://github.com/zepingyu0512/arithmetic-mechanism.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: The Same But Different: Structural Similarities and Differences in Multilingual Language Modeling
papers.research_question: When two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? When two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently. Moreover, we show that multilingual models employ language-specific components (attention heads and feed-forward networks) when needed to handle linguistic processes (e.g., morphological marking) that only exist in some languages. Together, our results provide new insights into how LLMs trade off between exploiting common structures and preserving linguistic differences when tasked with modeling multiple languages simultaneously.

papers.title: Positional Description Matters for Transformers Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How does positional encoding affect transformers' performance on arithmetic tasks, and how can we modify positional encoding or data representation to improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers' poor arithmetic performance stems from over-reliance on positional information, and proposes methods like padding, reversing products, and random embedding to improve performance, enabling small models to achieve high accuracy on large-digit multiplication and addition.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that with appropriate modifications to positional encoding or data format, small transformers can perform complex arithmetic tasks, highlighting the importance of positional information in arithmetic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Padding and reversing the product order enable a small transformer to perform 15-digit multiplication with high accuracy.
Using random spaces or recursive scratchpad formats improves length generalization in addition tasks.
Random embedding (a novel positional encoding) improves generalization for both digit reversion and addition tasks.
Integrating arithmetic data with natural language dialogue is challenging but can be improved by removing absolute positional embedding or using random embedding.
Including simple cases (like n×1 multiplication) in training helps models learn complex multiplication.
papers.limitation:
The experiments did not fine-tune hyperparameters, so higher accuracy for more digits might be possible with larger training sets, better digit distributions, or tuned learning rates.
The approaches for multiplication, length extrapolation, and natural language integration are tackled separately; a single model combining all properties is left for future work.
future_direction: Combining the proposed approaches into a single model that excels at all arithmetic challenges.
Exploring the methods on larger models and more complex arithmetic tasks.
papers.abstract: Transformers, central to the successes in modern Natural Language Processing, often falter on arithmetic tasks despite their vast capabilities --which paradoxically include remarkable coding abilities. We observe that a crucial challenge is their naive reliance on positional information to solve arithmetic problems with a small number of digits, leading to poor performance on larger numbers. Herein, we delve deeper into the role of positional encoding, and propose several ways to fix the issue, either by modifying the positional encoding directly, or by modifying the representation of the arithmetic task to leverage standard positional encoding differently. We investigate the value of these modifications for three tasks: (i) classical multiplication, (ii) length extrapolation in addition, and (iii) addition in natural language context. For (i) we train a small model on a small dataset (100M parameters and 300k samples) with remarkable aptitude in (direct, no scratchpad) 15 digits multiplication and essentially perfect up to 12 digits, while usual training in this context would give a model failing at 4 digits multiplication. In the experiments on addition, we use a mere 120k samples to demonstrate: for (ii) extrapolation from 10 digits to testing on 12 digits numbers while usual training would have no extrapolation, and for (iii) almost perfect accuracy up to 5 digits while usual training would be correct only up to 3 digits (which is essentially memorization with a training set of 120k samples).

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Does multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, with neuron overlap varying by category and influenced by language proximity and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models implicitly align morphosyntactic information across languages by using overlapping subsets of neurons, which may affect their cross-lingual transfer capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Significant cross-lingual overlap exists in neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
Overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and is lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Overlap is higher for languages within the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with pre-training data size but decreases with larger model size (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
XLM-R-base tends to share more neurons than m-BERT for encoding morphosyntactic attributes.
future_direction: Artificially encouraging neuron overlap to facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: The success of multilingual pre-trained models is underpinned by their ability to learn representations shared by multiple languages even in absence of any explicit supervision. However, it remains unclear how these models learn to generalise across languages. In this work, we conjecture that multilingual pre-trained models can derive language-universal abstractions about grammar. In particular, we investigate whether morphosyntactic information is encoded in the same subset of neurons in different languages. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study over 43 languages and 14 morphosyntactic categories with a state-of-the-art neuron-level probe. Our findings show that the cross-lingual overlap between neurons is significant, but its extent may vary across categories and depends on language proximity and pre-training data size.

papers.title: Interpreting and Improving Large Language Models in Arithmetic Calculation
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform arithmetic calculations, and can we improve their mathematical ability by fine-tuning specific components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that only a small fraction of attention heads and subsequent MLPs are responsible for arithmetic calculation in LLMs, and that selectively fine-tuning these components (Precise SFT) improves mathematical performance without degrading general abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies sparse attention heads and MLPs for arithmetic calculation in LLMs and shows that precise tuning of these components improves mathematical capability with less impact on non-mathematical tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small fraction (<5%) of attention heads are crucial for arithmetic calculation.
These heads attend to operands and operators.
Subsequent MLPs process the information to derive the answer.
The key components are transferable across datasets and tasks.
Precise fine-tuning of these components improves mathematical performance without harming general abilities.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily focus on LLaMA2 series, generalization to other LLMs needs further investigation.
The work focuses on arithmetic calculation, and more complex mathematical problems require further research.
future_direction: Generalize to a broader range of LLMs
Investigate more complex mathematical problems
Investigate shared and distinct mechanisms across mathematical tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential across numerous applications and have shown an emergent ability to tackle complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical computations. However, even for the simplest arithmetic calculations, the intrinsic mechanisms behind LLMs remain mysterious, making it challenging to ensure reliability. In this work, we delve into uncovering a specific mechanism by which LLMs execute calculations. Through comprehensive experiments, we find that LLMs frequently involve a small fraction (< 5%) of attention heads, which play a pivotal role in focusing on operands and operators during calculation processes. Subsequently, the information from these operands is processed through multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), progressively leading to the final solution. These pivotal heads/MLPs, though identified on a specific dataset, exhibit transferability across different datasets and even distinct tasks. This insight prompted us to investigate the potential benefits of selectively fine-tuning these essential heads/MLPs to boost the LLMs' computational performance. We empirically find that such precise tuning can yield notable enhancements on mathematical prowess, without compromising the performance on non-mathematical tasks. Our work serves as a preliminary exploration into the arithmetic calculation abilities inherent in LLMs, laying a solid foundation to reveal more intricate mathematical tasks.

papers.title: Cross-neutralising: Probing for joint encoding of linguistic information in multilingual models
papers.research_question: How are linguistic properties encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in multilingual models like M-BERT and XLM-R?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual models jointly encode typological linguistic properties across languages, and this can be probed using the cross-neutralising method.
papers.conclusion: Typological feature values are encoded jointly across languages in multilingual models and can be localized via language centroids.
papers.key_findings:
Self-neutralising by subtracting language centroids removes typological information, reducing probing accuracy to chance levels.
Cross-neutralising shows that performance deteriorates for languages sharing the same typological feature value, indicating joint encoding.
This joint encoding pattern is observed in both M-BERT and XLM-R models.
The effect is consistent across different layers of the models.
Language centroids capture specific feature values in a localizable way across languages.
papers.limitation: When probing performance before neutralising is low (<75% accuracy), it is unclear what information the language centroids capture, limiting the interpretation of results.
future_direction: Correlate typological feature encoding with downstream task performance
Use cross-neutralising for selective generalization in models based on typology
Apply the method to other scenarios like multimodal models
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders are widely used to transfer NLP models across languages. The success of this transfer is, however, dependent on the model's ability to encode the patterns of cross-lingual similarity and variation. Yet, little is known as to how these models are able to do this. We propose a simple method to study how relationships between languages are encoded in two state-of-the-art multilingual models (i.e. M-BERT and XLM-R). The results provide insight into their information sharing mechanisms and suggest that linguistic properties are encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in these models.

papers.title: On Representational Dissociation of Language and Arithmetic in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What about the language-thought dissociation in large language models? Specifically, are language and arithmetic inputs encoded in separate regions in LLMs' internal representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that language and arithmetic inputs are encoded in completely separated regions in LLMs' internal representation space, and that math word problems form a separate cluster, suggesting fine-grained modularity beyond a coarse language-arithmetic dissociation.
papers.conclusion: This study explores the representational dissociation between language and arithmetic stimuli in LLMs, setting a direction to bridge neuroscientific perspectives with LLM internal analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Language and arithmetic equations are encoded in completely separated regions across all layers of LLMs.
The separation is not due to token differences, as spelled-out equations are also separated from language inputs.
Math word problems (GSM8K) form a separate cluster from both language and arithmetic regions.
The arithmetic region activated with primitive stimuli is not used in more complex arithmetic-involved tasks.
There are numerous arithmetic regions for different task formats, indicating fine-grained modularity.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to geometrical properties of the representation space; causal analysis is needed to align with actual abilities.
The generality of findings could be enhanced with other methodologies, such as gradient descent, magnitude of neuron activations, or activation probability.
The topic should be addressed through different experimental designs, e.g., ablating language learning scenarios.
future_direction: Incorporate alternative approaches to identify language and arithmetic regions, such as gradient descent, magnitude of neuron activations, or activation probability.
Conduct causal analysis to test whether the observed geometrical dissociation aligns with actual abilities.
Contextualize the results with existing LM-brain alignment studies.
Address the learnability of specific abilities through different experimental designs, e.g., ablating language learning scenarios.
papers.abstract: The association between language and (non-linguistic) thinking ability in humans has long been debated, and recently, neuroscientific evidence of brain activity patterns has been considered. Such a scientific context naturally raises an interdisciplinary question -- what about such a language-thought dissociation in large language models (LLMs)? In this paper, as an initial foray, we explore this question by focusing on simple arithmetic skills (e.g., $1+2=$ ?) as a thinking ability and analyzing the geometry of their encoding in LLMs' representation space. Our experiments with linear classifiers and cluster separability tests demonstrate that simple arithmetic equations and general language input are encoded in completely separated regions in LLMs' internal representation space across all the layers, which is also supported with more controlled stimuli (e.g., spelled-out equations). These tentatively suggest that arithmetic reasoning is mapped into a distinct region from general language input, which is in line with the neuroscientific observations of human brain activations, while we also point out their somewhat cognitively implausible geometric properties.

papers.title: Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties in Language Models
papers.research_question: How are numeric properties (e.g., birth year, population) encoded in the internal representations of language models, and do these representations reflect the natural monotonic structure of such properties?
papers.core_contribution: Language models learn to represent numeric properties in low-dimensional, monotonic subspaces of their activation space, and these representations can be edited via activation patching to causally alter model output.
papers.conclusion: Language models learn monotonic representations of numeric properties, and such representations consistently emerge across different models, suggesting that pretraining captures the natural structure of numeric attributes.
papers.key_findings:
Low-dimensional subspaces (2-6 dimensions) of activation space are highly predictive (R^2 up to 0.91) of the numeric quantities a model expresses when queried.
Projections onto these subspaces reveal monotonic structure, where the position along a direction correlates with the value of the numeric attribute.
Activation patching along the found directions causally changes the model's output in a monotonic fashion, with the change in output correlating with the strength and sign of the intervention.
Monotonic representations of numeric properties exist across multiple language models (Llama 2, Falcon, Mistral) and multiple numeric properties (birth year, death year, population, elevation, latitude, longitude).
Editing along a direction for one property has side effects on other properties, suggesting some directions encode generic numeric ranges rather than being property-specific.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to popular entities, frequent numeric properties, and English queries.
Causal interventions via one-dimensional activation patching may be too simplistic, as properties are encoded in low- but not necessarily one-dimensional subspaces.
The ease of extracting information from representations is not fully quantified, and the intrinsic dimensionality of the models is unknown.
future_direction: What exactly do the found subspaces encode? Can we find more specific directions by adding constraints to minimize side effects?
Are changes along directions absolute or relative to typical value ranges?
Is the quality of numeric attribute representations connected to LM performance on tasks involving those attributes?
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) can express factual knowledge involving numeric properties such as Karl Popper was born in 1902. However, how this information is encoded in the model's internal representations is not understood well. Here, we introduce a simple method for finding and editing representations of numeric properties such as an entity's birth year. Empirically, we find low-dimensional subspaces that encode numeric properties monotonically, in an interpretable and editable fashion. When editing representations along directions in these subspaces, LM output changes accordingly. For example, by patching activations along a "birthyear" direction we can make the LM express an increasingly late birthyear: Karl Popper was born in 1929, Karl Popper was born in 1957, Karl Popper was born in 1968. Property-encoding directions exist across several numeric properties in all models under consideration, suggesting the possibility that monotonic representation of numeric properties consistently emerges during LM pretraining. Code: https://github.com/bheinzerling/numeric-property-repr

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Encoders Learn Cross-lingual Representation?
papers.research_question: How do multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations without explicit cross-lingual signals, and what factors influence this process?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation provides a comprehensive analysis of how multilingual encoders like mBERT learn cross-lingual representations, identifying key factors such as parameter sharing, anchor points, and language similarity, and proposes methods like contrastive alignment to improve cross-lingual transfer.
papers.conclusion: The thesis concludes that multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations through shared parameters and anchor points, but performance is uneven across languages, and explicit alignment can help. Future work includes scaling to more languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual BERT (mBERT) learns cross-lingual representations without any explicit cross-lingual signal, achieving strong zero-shot transfer across a variety of tasks.
Parameter sharing and anchor points (shared subwords across languages) are crucial for the emergence of cross-lingual representations in multilingual encoders.
Not all languages are equally represented in mBERT; low-resource languages suffer from poor performance due to limited pretraining data and vocabulary coverage.
Explicit alignment methods, such as contrastive alignment using bitext, can improve cross-lingual representations, but their effectiveness varies across models and language pairs.
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer exhibits high variance due to underspecified optimization, and data projection with self-training can constrain and improve transfer performance.
papers.limitation: mBERT performs poorly on low-resource languages due to limited pretraining data and vocabulary coverage.
future_direction: Continue scaling multilingual encoders to more languages and larger models
Extend to multimodal multilingual models
Improve cross-lingual transfer for low-resource languages
papers.abstract: NLP systems typically require support for more than one language. As different languages have different amounts of supervision, cross-lingual transfer benefits languages with little to no training data by transferring from other languages. From an engineering perspective, multilingual NLP benefits development and maintenance by serving multiple languages with a single system. Both cross-lingual transfer and multilingual NLP rely on cross-lingual representations serving as the foundation. As BERT revolutionized representation learning and NLP, it also revolutionized cross-lingual representations and cross-lingual transfer. Multilingual BERT was released as a replacement for single-language BERT, trained with Wikipedia data in 104 languages. Surprisingly, without any explicit cross-lingual signal, multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual representations in addition to representations for individual languages. This thesis first shows such surprising cross-lingual effectiveness compared against prior art on various tasks. Naturally, it raises a set of questions, most notably how do these multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations. In exploring these questions, this thesis will analyze the behavior of multilingual models in a variety of settings on high and low resource languages. We also look at how to inject different cross-lingual signals into multilingual encoders, and the optimization behavior of cross-lingual transfer with these models. Together, they provide a better understanding of multilingual encoders on cross-lingual transfer. Our findings will lead us to suggested improvements to multilingual encoders and cross-lingual transfer.

papers.title: Unraveling Arithmetic in Large Language Models: The Role of Algebraic Structures
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) learn to perform arithmetic operations? Specifically, do they capture underlying algebraic structures like commutativity and identity from input-output relationships?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes that LLMs learn arithmetic by capturing algebraic structures such as commutativity and identity from input-output relationships, rather than by directly encoding numerical values. It provides both empirical evidence using custom datasets and a theoretical construction showing transformer-based models can be configured to exhibit invariance to input permutations and identity element insertion.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can internalize algebraic structures like commutativity and identity from training data, providing a foundation for understanding and potentially enhancing their arithmetic capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can learn and generalize the commutative and identity properties of operators from training data to unseen inputs.
The learning is operator-specific; models can distinguish between operators that have these properties (like '+') and those that do not (like '⊖').
Performance on a synthetic operator '⊕' shows that LLMs learn these algebraic structures without relying on underlying numerical calculations of the input indices.
Learning commutativity requires a larger training set size than learning identity or non-commutative operators, but the required size is still much smaller than the full combinatorial space.
All tested tasks, including learning commutative and identity properties for '+' and '⊕' and learning non-commutative operators '⊖', '⊳', and '⊲', eventually achieve over 99% testing accuracy with sufficient training data.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable mathematical capabilities, largely driven by chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, which decomposes complex reasoning into step-by-step solutions. This approach has enabled significant advancements, as evidenced by performance on benchmarks like GSM8K and MATH. However, the mechanisms underlying LLMs' ability to perform arithmetic in a single step of CoT remain poorly understood. Existing studies debate whether LLMs encode numerical values or rely on symbolic reasoning, while others explore attention and multi-layered processing in arithmetic tasks. In this work, we propose that LLMs learn arithmetic by capturing algebraic structures, such as commutativity and identity properties. Since these structures are observable through input-output relationships, they can generalize to unseen data. We empirically demonstrate that LLMs can learn algebraic structures using a custom dataset of arithmetic problems, as well as providing theoretical evidence showing that, under specific configurations of weights and biases, the transformer-based LLMs can generate embeddings that remain invariant to both permutations of input tokens and the presence of identity elements. Our findings indicate that leveraging algebraic structures can enhance the LLMs' arithmetic capabilities, offering insights into improving their arithmetic performance.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Sequence Continuation: Analyzing Shared Circuits in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether large language models re-use shared circuits for similar sequence continuation tasks, such as Arabic numerals, number words, and months.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that large language models re-use shared sub-circuits for similar sequence continuation tasks, and shows that these circuits have analogous functionality across different models like GPT-2 Small and Llama-2-7B.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that transformers leverage shared computational structures across similar tasks, advancing the understanding of how they represent abstract concepts and contributing to mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Shared sub-circuits exist for similar sequence continuation tasks in both GPT-2 Small and Llama-2-7B.
Key components include attention heads for sequence member detection (e.g., head 4.4) and successor prediction (e.g., head 9.1), as well as MLP 9 for next member calculation.
These circuits affect a wide range of math-related prompts, including intervaled sequences and arithmetic tasks.
The functionality of components is consistent across tasks, indicating re-use of computational structures.
Analogous sub-circuits are found in different models, suggesting common mechanisms for sequence processing.
future_direction: Examine if shared circuits appear in more models
Expand studies on non-linear features and their effects on math-related circuits
papers.abstract: While transformer models exhibit strong capabilities on linguistic tasks, their complex architectures make them difficult to interpret. Recent work has aimed to reverse engineer transformer models into human-readable representations called circuits that implement algorithmic functions. We extend this research by analyzing and comparing circuits for similar sequence continuation tasks, which include increasing sequences of Arabic numerals, number words, and months. By applying circuit interpretability analysis, we identify a key sub-circuit in both GPT-2 Small and Llama-2-7B responsible for detecting sequence members and for predicting the next member in a sequence. Our analysis reveals that semantically related sequences rely on shared circuit subgraphs with analogous roles. Additionally, we show that this sub-circuit has effects on various math-related prompts, such as on intervaled circuits, Spanish number word and months continuation, and natural language word problems. Overall, documenting shared computational structures enables better model behavior predictions, identification of errors, and safer editing procedures. This mechanistic understanding of transformers is a critical step towards building more robust, aligned, and interpretable language models.

papers.title: What Language(s) Does Aya-23 Think In? How Multilinguality Affects Internal Language Representations
papers.research_question: How does balanced multilingual training affect internal language processing in LLMs, specifically in terms of language activation, neuron sharing, and layer-wise distribution of language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Balanced multilingual training leads to distinct internal language processing, with language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of typologically related languages during translation, unlike English-centric models.
papers.conclusion: Balanced multilingual training fundamentally alters how decoder-only LLMs process language internally, leading to language-specific neurons concentrated in final layers and activation of multiple languages during translation.
papers.key_findings:
Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language.
Code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one.
Aya-23’s language-specific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models.
Neuron overlap analysis shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types.
French-based code-mixed inputs show higher neuron clustering than Chinese-based inputs across all models, regardless of training data composition.
papers.limitation:
Token overlap between languages in the logit lens experiments may affect analysis of language-specific activation patterns.
Neuron specialization analysis using binary activations results in information loss that may obscure subtle activation patterns.
Code-mixed dataset created via rule-based word-to-word translation produces unnatural sentences that may not represent authentic code-switching.
Analysis is limited to three models and may not generalize to other architectures or sizes.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multilingual tasks, yet their internal language processing remains poorly understood. We analyze how Aya-23-8B, a decoder-only LLM trained on balanced multilingual data, handles code-mixed, cloze, and translation tasks compared to predominantly monolingual models like Llama 3 and Chinese-LLaMA-2. Using logit lens and neuron specialization analyses, we find: (1) Aya-23 activates typologically related language representations during translation, unlike English-centric models that rely on a single pivot language; (2) code-mixed neuron activation patterns vary with mixing rates and are shaped more by the base language than the mixed-in one; and (3) Aya-23's languagespecific neurons for code-mixed inputs concentrate in final layers, diverging from prior findings on decoder-only models. Neuron overlap analysis further shows that script similarity and typological relations impact processing across model types. These findings reveal how multilingual training shapes LLM internals and inform future cross-lingual transfer research.

papers.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs form shared representations across languages with language-specific decoding, and why does performance favor the dominant training language such as English?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs form a shared language-agnostic representation space in middle layers, with language-specific decoding in late layers; performance gaps are mechanistically explained by tokenizer bias and feature strength differences.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs use shared representations in middle layers and language-specific decoding in late layers, with performance gaps explained by feature strength and tokenizer bias.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs consistently form a shared language-agnostic space in middle layers, regardless of English dominance in training data.
Language-specific decoding depends on a small set of high-frequency features in late layers that linearly encode language identity from early layers.
Non-English performance failures are linked to dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias forcing early layers to specialize in word reassembly.
Finetuning strengthens these features and their connections, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding.
The shared multilingual space emerges as an architectural property, even when models are trained without English.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) can process many languages, yet how they internally represent this diversity remains unclear. Do they form shared multilingual representations with language-specific decoding, and if so, why does performance favor the dominant training language? To address this, we train models on different multilingual mixtures and analyze their internal mechanisms using Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) and Attribution Graphs. Our results reveal multilingual shared representations: the model employs highly similar features across languages, while language-specific decoding emerges in later layers. Training models without English shows identical multilingual shared space structures. Decoding relies partly on a small set of high-frequency features in the final layers, which linearly encode language identity from early layers. Intervening on these features allows one language to be suppressed and another substituted. Finally, to explain non-English failures, we perform a Model-Diffing experiment: underperformance arises from dim late-layer features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer bias toward English that forces early layers to specialize in word reassembly. Finetuning strengthens these features and their links, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding, providing a mechanistic explanation for multilingual gaps. Our models and CLTs are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-clts and https://huggingface.co/collections/CausalNLP/multilingual-gpt2-models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/abirharrasse/MultilingualCLTs

papers.title: Learning-induced reorganization of number neurons and emergence of numerical representations in a biologically inspired neural network
papers.research_question: How does numerosity training reorganize neuronal tuning properties and population-level representations in a biologically inspired neural network?
papers.core_contribution: Numerosity training reorganizes neuronal tuning and population representations, leading to the emergence of sharp numerosity tuning and latent magnitude representations in a biologically inspired neural network.
papers.conclusion: Our findings elucidate mechanisms by which learning builds novel representations supporting number sense.
papers.key_findings:
Numerosity training reorganizes spontaneous number neurons (SPONs), with most SPONs dropping or switching their preferred numerosity.
Training increases tuning precision, stability, and selectivity of number-sensitive neurons, especially in the IPS layer.
Ablation shows that persistent SPONs are not critical for numerosity classification; newly trained and switched neurons are more important.
Representational similarity analysis reveals increased differentiation between numerosities after training.
Multidimensional scaling reveals latent representations of absolute magnitude and relative magnitude (midpoint anchoring) post-training.
papers.abstract: Number sense, the ability to decipher quantity, forms the foundation for mathematical cognition. How number sense emerges with learning is, however, not known. Here we use a biologically-inspired neural architecture comprising cortical layers V1, V2, V3, and intraparietal sulcus (IPS) to investigate how neural representations change with numerosity training. Learning dramatically reorganized neuronal tuning properties at both the single unit and population levels, resulting in the emergence of sharply-tuned representations of numerosity in the IPS layer. Ablation analysis revealed that spontaneous number neurons observed prior to learning were not critical to formation of number representations post-learning. Crucially, multidimensional scaling of population responses revealed the emergence of absolute and relative magnitude representations of quantity, including mid-point anchoring. These learnt representations may underlie changes from logarithmic to cyclic and linear mental number lines that are characteristic of number sense development in humans. Our findings elucidate mechanisms by which learning builds novel representations supporting number sense.

papers.title: Investigating the Potential of Task Arithmetic for Cross-Lingual Transfer
papers.research_question: Can task arithmetic, a method for editing pretrained models using multiple full fine-tunings, be applied to achieve modular cross-lingual transfer?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that task arithmetic can be effectively applied to cross-lingual transfer, enabling modular combination of language and task vectors from full fine-tunings to achieve strong zero-shot transfer, particularly for low-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: Task arithmetic is a potent and modular approach for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, effectively combining language and task vectors derived from full fine-tuning to specialize models for specific language-task pairs.
papers.key_findings:
Task arithmetic with language and task vector addition (+TGT variant) yields substantial performance gains (up to 12 points) on low-resource language benchmarks like AmericasNLI and NusaX over a standard fully fine-tuned model.
The method achieves competitive or improved performance compared to state-of-the-art parameter-efficient cross-lingual transfer methods like Sparse Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Target Language-Ready (TLR) adapters.
Scaling factors for language vectors significantly impact performance, and optimal values vary across tasks and languages.
Imposing sparsity on language vectors generally degrades performance, indicating that a more refined approach is needed for sparsity to be beneficial in this context.
The task analogy variant (-SRC +TGT) underperforms compared to simply adding the target language vector, suggesting that source language knowledge is valuable and should not be suppressed.
papers.limitation:
The work is a short paper with page constraints, limiting the extent and depth of experiments and analysis.
All results are based on a single run due to the large number of languages and methods, though averaging over many targets and replication with two models enhances confidence.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to different model types (e.g., encoder-decoder models) and in few-shot cross-lingual transfer scenarios.
Develop more nuanced, per-parameter weighting methods for the vectors, potentially using Fisher information.
Investigate more refined sparsity approaches for language vectors, possibly involving re-training or sophisticated parameter selection.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual transfer has recently been tackled through modular, parameter-efficient finetuning methods which allow arbitrary combinations of language and task modules for transfer of any task to any language.Concurrently, task arithmetic has emerged as a powerful and modular tool for editing pretrained models using multiple full fine-tunings.In this work, we connect the paradigms of task arithmetic and crosslingual transfer, demonstrating that modularity for cross-lingual transfer can be achieved even with full model fine-tuning.Our approach displays strong performance on a range of multilingual benchmarks encompassing both highresource and low-resource languages.

papers.title: Probing for Arithmetic Errors in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal activations in language models be used to detect arithmetic errors?
papers.core_contribution: Simple probes can detect arithmetic errors from internal activations and enable lightweight self-correction via re-prompting.
papers.conclusion: Simple probes can extract predicted outputs and correct answers from internal activations, anticipate errors, generalize to chain-of-thought, and serve as weak oracles for self-correction.
papers.key_findings:
Probes can decode both the model's predicted output and the correct answer from hidden states with high accuracy.
Error detectors trained on these probes achieve over 90% accuracy in predicting model correctness.
Probes trained on simple arithmetic generalize to chain-of-thought reasoning on GSM8K problems.
Using error detectors to guide re-prompting corrects up to 11% of erroneous reasoning steps without degrading correct outputs.
Internal representations of numerical quantities are robust across contexts, enabling cross-setting generalization.
papers.limitation:
Focus on addition and subtraction, not other arithmetic operations like multiplication or division.
Experiments primarily on Gemma 2B IT, with limited evaluation on Phi-3.
Chain-of-thought analysis limited to addition-only GSM8K problems.
CoT evaluation uses structured equation formatting, not free-form natural language.
future_direction: Extend probing strategies to other arithmetic operations such as multiplication and division.
Broader evaluation across diverse architectures and model scales.
Explore other datasets with broader math coverage and varied reasoning formats.
Extend approach to operate over general, unstructured CoT traces.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether internal activations in language models can be used to detect arithmetic errors. Starting with a controlled setting of 3-digit addition, we show that simple probes can accurately decode both the model's predicted output and the correct answer from hidden states, regardless of whether the model's output is correct. Building on this, we train lightweight error detectors that predict model correctness with over 90% accuracy. We then extend our analysis to structured chain-of-thought traces on addition-only GSM8K problems and find that probes trained on simple arithmetic generalize well to this more complex setting, revealing consistent internal representations. Finally, we demonstrate that these probes can guide selective re-prompting of erroneous reasoning steps, improving task accuracy with minimal disruption to correct outputs. Our findings suggest that arithmetic errors can be anticipated from internal activations alone, and that simple probes offer a viable path toward lightweight model self-correction.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How is syntactic agreement encoded in multilingual language models, and to what extent are syntax neurons shared across languages and syntactic structures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds two distinct layer-wise patterns for syntactic agreement depending on dependency distance, significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual models but not in masked language models, and that syntax neurons are shared across structures but not with semantic baselines.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that multilingual language models encode syntactic agreement in similar ways across languages, with distinct mechanisms for short- and long-range dependencies, and that causal probing reveals a richer syntactic sensitivity than behavioral analyses suggest.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct layer-wise NIE patterns exist for short-range and long-range syntactic agreement.
Neuron overlap across languages is significant in autoregressive multilingual models (XGLM) but not in masked language models (mBERT).
Neurons are shared across syntactic structures but not with semantic plausibility or bigram collocation baselines.
Syntax neurons are more sparse in masked language models than in autoregressive language models.
Behavioral analyses likely underestimate the sensitivity of masked language models to syntactic information due to negative interference from other neurons.
papers.limitation:
The method is limited to stimuli where subjects and verbs are single tokens, restricting the range of words and languages that can be studied.
Analyzing individual neurons may oversimplify the encoding of complex phenomena like syntactic agreement, which likely involves sets of neurons.
future_direction: Develop probing methods that allow for variable-length span predictions.
Focus on non-parametric methods that probe multiple neurons simultaneously to causally implicate model regions.
papers.abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models' subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.

papers.title: Exploring Early Number Abilities With Multimodal Transformers
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the order in which a multimodal transformer model acquires early number tasks, compares its behavior to human data, and analyzes how input modality affects task specialization and representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a multimodal transformer model can learn early number tasks with trajectories similar to children's cognitive development, and exhibits psychophysical effects like size and distance effects.
papers.conclusion: The multimodal transformer model's learning trajectories align with empirical data from children, and it exhibits classic numerical effects, providing insights into numerical cognition.
papers.key_findings:
The model acquires tasks in an order reflecting input length and variability, aligning with educational psychology findings.
It displays symbolic and non-symbolic size and distance effects in number comparisons.
Using the logit lens, tasks are solved at different attention layers, indicating varying difficulty.
Models trained without symbolic inputs use more processing-intensive strategies for set size determination.
The model's performance on give-N tasks shows a progression similar to knower-level stages in children.
papers.limitation: The model's performance on larger numerosities increases due to the limited range of numerosities used, which is an artifact.
papers.abstract: Early number skills represent critical milestones in children's cognitive development and are shaped over years of interacting with quantities and numerals in various contexts. Several connectionist computational models have attempted to emulate how certain number concepts may be learned, represented, and processed in the brain. However, these models mainly used highly simplified inputs and focused on limited tasks. We expand on previous work in two directions: First, we train a model end-to-end on video demonstrations in a synthetic environment with multimodal visual and language inputs. Second, we use a more holistic dataset of 35 tasks, covering enumeration, set comparisons, symbolic digits, and seriation. The order in which the model acquires tasks reflects input length and variability, and the resulting trajectories mostly fit with findings from educational psychology. The trained model also displays symbolic and non-symbolic size and distance effects. Using techniques from interpretability research, we investigate how our attention-based model integrates cross-modal representations and binds them into context-specific associative networks to solve different tasks. We compare models trained with and without symbolic inputs and find that the purely non-symbolic model employs more processing-intensive strategies to determine set size.

papers.title: Language Arithmetics: Towards Systematic Language Neuron Identification and Manipulation
papers.research_question: How do language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs control language behavior, and can they be manipulated to steer model outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language arithmetics, an additive neuron intervention method, to identify and manipulate language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs, showing that it can steer language generation and improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Our large-scale study demonstrates that language-specific neurons encode meaningful linguistic features that can be identified, analyzed, and manipulated to steer model behavior across languages. By employing a novel additive intervention method, we show that activating these neurons allows for generation language control and improves performance on various multilingual tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization.
Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting linguistic proximity.
Additive language arithmetics outperforms replacement-based methods for language forcing.
Activating target-language neurons improves performance on multilingual tasks like translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI.
Models exhibit internal 'fallback' mechanisms for language selection when dominant language neurons are deactivated.
papers.limitation:
Broader evaluation across more diverse downstream settings is needed.
Quality and fluency of forced outputs across languages, especially low-resource ones, remain underexplored.
Analysis focuses on isolated neurons, overlooking distributed representations and circuits.
Computational constraints limited some experiments to smaller models.
future_direction: Investigate the interactions and dependencies between neurons to understand network-level mechanisms supporting multilingual processing.
More detailed investigation of language fallback dynamics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual abilities, yet the neural mechanisms behind language-specific processing remain unclear. We analyze language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, and Aya-Expanse-8B & 32B across 21 typologically diverse languages, identifying neurons that control language behavior. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy (LAPE) method, we show that these neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization. Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting internal representations of linguistic proximity. Through language arithmetics, i.e. systematic activation addition and multiplication, we steer models to deactivate unwanted languages and activate desired ones, outperforming simpler replacement approaches. These interventions effectively guide behavior across five multilingual tasks: language forcing, translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI. Manipulation is more successful for high-resource languages, while typological similarity improves effectiveness. We also demonstrate that cross-lingual neuron steering enhances downstream performance and reveal internal "fallback" mechanisms for language selection when neurons are progressively deactivated. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/d-gurgurov/Language-Neurons-Manipulation.

papers.title: No Train but Gain: Language Arithmetic for training-free Language Adapters enhancement
papers.research_question: How can we enhance language adapters in multilingual models to improve cross-lingual performance without additional training, addressing the trade-off between positive transfer and negative interference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces language arithmetic, a training-free post-processing method that enhances language adapters by combining them via weighted addition, improving cross-lingual performance especially in zero-shot and low-resource scenarios.
papers.conclusion: Language arithmetic is an effective training-free method for enhancing language adapters, particularly beneficial in zero-shot and low-resource settings, and highlights differences between language and task arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
Language arithmetic consistently improves over proxy baselines in zero-shot scenarios, with gains up to 3.1 F1 points.
It also improves existing language adapters, with significant gains in low-resource regimes and for languages not seen during pre-training.
The method is robust to the choice of the lambda parameter; a coarse search (step 0.1 or 0.2) is sufficient, and setting lambda=0.5 is near optimal.
Language vectors have higher cosine similarity than task vectors, indicating different properties and making techniques like Ties-Merging less effective for multilingual adapter merging.
Language arithmetic outperforms Ties-Merging in the multilingual context, as pruning (which helps for task vectors) decreases performance for language vectors.
papers.limitation:
The work was tested on English-centric task training and could be extended to different languages with more PEFT methods.
Applying multi-source training could provide better robustness of the task adapters and a more thorough analysis.
future_direction: Extend language arithmetic by incorporating more components into the sum.
Adapt other elements of the task arithmetic framework (task analogies and forgetting via negation) to a multilingual setup.
Evaluate LA's performance on various non-classification tasks.
papers.abstract: Modular deep learning is the state-of-the-art solution for lifting the curse of multilinguality, preventing the impact of negative interference and enabling cross-lingual performance in Multilingual Pre-trained Language Models. However, a trade-off of this approach is the reduction in positive transfer learning from closely related languages. In response, we introduce a novel method called language arithmetic, which enables training-free post-processing to address this limitation. Extending the task arithmetic framework, we apply learning via addition to the language adapters, transitioning the framework from a multi-task to a multilingual setup. The effectiveness of the proposed solution is demonstrated on three downstream tasks in a MAD-X-based set of cross-lingual schemes, acting as a post-processing procedure. Language arithmetic consistently improves the baselines with significant gains, especially in the most challenging case of zero-shot application. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/mklimasz/language-arithmetic .

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how multilingual language models acquire and represent factual knowledge across languages, specifically examining the factors affecting probing performance, whether fact representations are shared or independent across languages, and how cross-lingual representations are formed.
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes methods for distinguishing three types of fact representations in multilingual language models (language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred) and reveals the challenges in cross-lingual factual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: Our research establishes the groundwork for further studies in understanding cross-lingual factual knowledge representation and highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages in ML-LMs.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance across languages shows moderate correlation with training data volume and strong negative correlation with mask token count.
There are localized knowledge sharing patterns among geographically proximate languages.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations, even for the same fact.
Active fact neurons in low-resource languages are more active and distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
Cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge does occur but is limited, and many correctly predicted facts in low-resource languages can be attributed to simple inference patterns rather than true transfer.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R) and may not generalize to large decoder-based multilingual models.
future_direction: Enhance the cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs).In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge.Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT).We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts.We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: languageindependent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them.Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs. 1

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 2.1, Grade-School Math and the Hidden Reasoning Process
papers.research_question: How do language models solve grade-school math problems? Do they memorize templates or learn reasoning skills? What is the hidden reasoning process and what causes mistakes?
papers.core_contribution: Language models trained on synthetic grade-school math problems can learn reasoning skills, generalize to longer reasoning lengths, and internally compute unnecessary dependencies, indicating learning beyond the training objective.
papers.conclusion: Language models can learn genuine reasoning skills from synthetic data, and depth is more important than width for reasoning ability.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy and generalize to longer reasoning lengths than seen during training.
Models generate shortest solutions, avoiding unnecessary computations, suggesting planning.
Probing reveals the model preprocesses necessary parameters before generation.
Models learn to compute all-pair dependencies, a skill not required by the training data.
Mistakes can be explained by probing internal states and are sometimes predictable.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not directly apply to foundation models like GPT-4 or more challenging mathematical reasoning tasks.
Uses synthetic data with modulo arithmetic, which may not reflect real-world math problems.
future_direction: Physics of Language Models: Part 2.2, How to Learn From Mistakes on Grade-School Math Problems
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language models have demonstrated their capability to solve mathematical reasoning problems, achieving near-perfect accuracy on grade-school level math benchmarks like GSM8K. In this paper, we formally study how language models solve these problems. We design a series of controlled experiments to address several fundamental questions: (1) Can language models truly develop reasoning skills, or do they simply memorize templates? (2) What is the model's hidden (mental) reasoning process? (3) Do models solve math questions using skills similar to or different from humans? (4) Do models trained on GSM8K-like datasets develop reasoning skills beyond those necessary for solving GSM8K problems? (5) What mental process causes models to make reasoning mistakes? (6) How large or deep must a model be to effectively solve GSM8K-level math questions? Our study uncovers many hidden mechanisms by which language models solve mathematical questions, providing insights that extend beyond current understandings of LLMs.

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? How do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance relate to the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization analysis tool for comparing multilingual and monolingual representations, and uses it to study morphosyntactic feature encoding across 33 languages and 17 categories, finding variations across layers and language properties.
papers.conclusion: The introduced tool provides insights into language representation in multilingual models and has practical implications for improving performance in cross-lingual tasks. Future work will extend the analysis to multimodal models.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information varies across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties such as writing system and number of unique characters.
Logographic writing systems (Chinese, Japanese) lead to distinct representations and present unique challenges for multilingual models.
Multilingual representations show distinct encoding patterns in subsets of languages with low language proximity.
Representation of low-resource languages benefits from the presence of related languages.
Factorization outputs yield a phylogenetic tree structure similar to linguists' trees and correlate with cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R, not other models like BERT, mBERT, T5, mT5 due to computational resources.
Downsampled Wikipedia to 200MB per language, though validated with a public XLM-R checkpoint.
Analyses limited to morphosyntactic features, plan to expand to semantics and pragmatics.
future_direction: Extend the analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand the analysis to other linguistic aspects, such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, enabling targeted extraction of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by causal effects on language modeling performance and direct subspace comparisons.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages.
Stable language-neutral axes encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech, and these axes are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
The identified axes (both language-sensitive and language-neutral) are relatively stable across middle layers of the model.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures like spirals, toruses, and curves in the representation space.
future_direction: Investigate how nonlinear structures (e.g., spirals, toruses) arise from and interact with the dot product self-attention mechanism in Transformer models.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.

Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically, and the extent to which representation spaces can be fully decomposed into orthogonal subspaces encoding different features.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: Carrying over algorithm in transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformer models implement the carrying over algorithm for integer addition, and how are the tasks allocated to different network components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer models implement the carrying over algorithm for integer addition in a modular fashion, with specific layers handling digit addition, carry decision, and carry addition.
papers.conclusion: Transformers implement the carrying over algorithm in a modular way, and insights from small models can inform understanding of larger models and improve generalization.
papers.key_findings:
For two-layer encoder-only models, the carrying over algorithm is implemented modularly with the first layer adding digits, the second layer deciding where to carry, and the MLP adding the carried one.
The same implementation is found in three-layer and decoder-only models.
Suggestive evidence indicates similar mechanisms in large language models like Alpaca 7B, Llemma 7B, and Zephyr 7B.
